name: OMAD (one meal a day)

lead: OMAD means one meal a day, usually in a one- to two-hour window. It is a form of intermittent fasting used to cut body fat and get a leaner look with one simple rule.

Compressing eating into one window tends to lower total daily intake, which produces a calorie deficit. Broader intermittent fasting research shows modest weight loss, with limited evidence that it outperforms continuous calorie restriction, and no trials specific to OMAD and appearance were found.

paras: People eat a single large meal and fast the rest of the day, drinking only calorie-free drinks. It is sometimes combined with low-carbohydrate eating or fat-loss drugs, and with resistance training to hold muscle.

Short-term hunger, irritability, dizziness and headaches are reported. Health bodies advise against intermittent fasting for pregnant women, children, older adults, underweight people and those with eating disorders.

angle.text: Users eat all daily food in one sitting as a simple way to run a calorie deficit and lean out. It is a form of time-restricted eating, and no trials have tested OMAD specifically for appearance.

lead: OMAD stands for "one meal a day", an eating pattern in which all daily food is consumed in a single sitting, usually within a one- to two-hour window, with water, other non-caloric drinks, vitamins, minerals and medication taken during the rest of the day.[1][2] Wikipedia classifies it as the narrowest form of time-restricted eating within the wider family of intermittent fasting.[1]

People use it to look leaner. Eating once a day compresses the whole day's calories into one meal, which many dieters find an easier way to hold a calorie deficit than counting several small meals. Lower body fat is what reveals jaw, cheekbone and eye-area definition in the face and muscle definition in the physique, which is why forum users running a cut often reach for it, sometimes alongside resistance training, a low-carbohydrate diet, or fat-loss drugs.[3][4]

The research base concerns intermittent fasting in general. Reviews of intermittent-fasting trials in overweight adults report weight loss in the range of 2.5 to 9.9 percent, with limited evidence that it differs from ordinary calorie restriction; a 2019 review in the New England Journal of Medicine described the field as promising but uncertain for long-term outcomes.[1][5] Two controlled studies bear most directly on eating once a day or in a narrow window: a randomized crossover trial of one meal versus three meals at equal calories, and a 12-week randomized trial of 16:8 time-restricted eating.[6][6] No trial has tested OMAD for facial appearance.

paras: In time-restricted eating, food is limited to a daily window often of 8 to 12 hours; OMAD narrows this to about one to two hours.[1] Wikipedia describes the pattern as eating the day's food in a single sitting, with water, other non-caloric drinks, vitamins, minerals and medication allowed during the remaining hours.[2] The meal itself is usually large, and the fast that precedes it is typically about 22 to 23 hours.

Other intermittent-fasting schedules differ in how they cut intake. Alternate-day fasting alternates a fast day of under 25 percent of usual energy needs with a normal feast day. The 5:2 diet allows roughly 500 to 600 calories on two non-consecutive days a week and was first documented in a 2011 article co-authored by Michelle Harvie and Mark Mattson, then popularised by Michael Mosley after the 2012 BBC Horizon documentary Eat, Fast and Live Longer.[1] OMAD instead repeats the same short window every day.

Fasting is an ancient practice found in many cultures and religions, including Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, Jainism and Judaism.[1] Therapeutic intermittent fasts for obesity have been investigated since at least 1915, and medical interest revived in the 1960s after Bloom and colleagues published an enthusiastic report on fasts of one to fourteen days. Enthusiasm spread into lay magazines, which led researchers and clinicians to caution against fasting without medical monitoring.[1]

Intermittent fasting became a trend in Silicon Valley and was ranked the most popular diet of 2018 in a survey by the International Food Information Council, according to Wikipedia.[1] By 2019 companies were selling fasting coaching, supplements and meal packages, and critics said some of these products were expensive and not supported by science.[1]

OMAD circulates as its own named routine in online fitness and weight-loss communities, valued for simplicity: one meal, no meal planning for the rest of the day, and a large dinner to look forward to. Lifters on T Nation log OMAD periods alongside training, describing it as fitting their schedule, with one poster saying he had been "flying" on a fasting, low-frequency format.[7][8][9] Looksmaxxing forums discuss it chiefly as a cutting tool.

The appeal for looks is fat loss. A single large meal can make it simpler to stay under a calorie target, and people cutting before or after a bulk describe it as a way to get lean enough to show facial and muscular definition.[3][4] Forum members discuss pairing OMAD with resistance training[3] or with GLP-1 drugs[4] as part of a cut.

Some posters also describe a cosmetic benefit of morning flatness: one thread claims that eating once, late in the day, avoids morning bloating and a puffier-looking face.[10] That is a personal observation shared on the forum rather than a studied outcome.

Proponents of intermittent fasting point to the sequence of metabolic states described in the research literature: after a meal the body relies on glucose for roughly four hours, then draws on liver glycogen, and after about 12 to 36 hours of fasting shifts toward mobilising fat and producing ketones, a transition some authors call the metabolic switch.[1] They connect this to fat loss and, in animal research, to broader effects on ageing and disease that de Cabo and Mattson review.[5]

Practical arguments are also common: fewer decisions, no snacking, bigger and more satisfying meals, and less time spent preparing food. On looksmax.org one poster called OMAD a "cheat code" for weight loss, reporting good energy and manageable hunger at 1,000 to 1,300 kcal while training.[3]

No clinical trials of OMAD as a fat-loss method for appearance were found. Studies of intermittent fasting more broadly report weight loss of about 2.5 to 9.9 percent in most trials, with limited evidence that it matches continuous calorie restriction, and with dropout rates of 2 to 38 percent against 0 to 50 percent for calorie restriction.[1] A 2026 review discusses impacts, mechanisms and cautions of intermittent fasting across medical and lifestyle domains.[11]

One-meal trial. A randomized crossover trial by Carlson and colleagues gave healthy, normal-weight adults the same total calories either as three meals or as one meal per day, in two 8-week periods separated by an 11-week break. During the one-meal period participants showed higher morning fasting glucose, larger and longer-lasting rises in blood glucose after a glucose drink, and a delayed insulin response; ghrelin, a hunger-related hormone, was higher. Fasting insulin, leptin, adiponectin and resistin did not change significantly, and the glucose-tolerance changes were reversible.[6]

Time-restricted eating trial. The TREAT trial randomized 116 adults with overweight or obesity to 16:8 time-restricted eating or three structured meals a day for 12 weeks. The time-restricted group lost 0.94 kg and the control group 0.68 kg, a difference the authors found not significant; in a subgroup with in-person measurements, appendicular lean mass index differed between groups, and the authors concluded that time-restricted eating alone was not more effective for weight loss than eating throughout the day.[6]

Reviews summarised by Wikipedia report that intermittent fasting may reduce waist circumference, fat mass, LDL cholesterol, triglycerides and fasting insulin, may slightly lower systolic blood pressure, and produces weight loss comparable to ordinary calorie restriction; for time-restricted eating the ratio of fat mass to lean mass lost is about 4 to 1.[1] A 2025 review cited there found no consistent effect of a 12-hour fast on cognitive performance, and a 2019 review found no athletic performance benefit, with overnight-fasted exercise reducing performance in efforts longer than 60 minutes.[1][2] The 2019 NEJM review called the science on long-term effects preliminary and uncertain.[5]
A 2025 case report in the Journal of Family Medicine and Primary Care described a 42-year-old man with prediabetes and class III obesity managed through one meal a day.[12]

Short-term effects of intermittent fasting include hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea, headaches and impaired thinking, usually fading within a month.[1] It is not recommended for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children and adolescents, older adults, underweight people, or those with or prone to eating disorders.[1]

Wikipedia notes that preliminary evidence suggests intermittent fasting is generally safe for people without diabetes or eating disorders, that the New Zealand Ministry of Health advises against it for people with insulin-dependent diabetes, and that the US National Institute on Aging says research is too limited to recommend it to the general public.[2] The American Heart Association says there is no good evidence of heart-health benefits, and the American Diabetes Association found limited evidence on safety and effects in type 1 diabetes.[1] The NHS advises people considering the 5:2 diet to consult a physician first.[1]

A concern raised in lifting circles and on looksmax.org is muscle retention: some posters argue that a single meal means too little protein stimulation for muscle building. The TREAT trial's lean-mass finding in its in-person subgroup is the closest published data point, and no trial has tested OMAD in people training for muscle.[6]

Users on looksmax.org describe OMAD as easier to sustain than several small meals.[3] Others ask whether OMAD at about 1,500 kcal causes hair loss, with replies suggesting that extreme deficits rather than moderate ones do.[13] Threads also compare OMAD with water fasting for rapid fat loss before a bulk, and ask whether it raises growth hormone.[4][14]

A common thread across posts is that OMAD is a delivery mechanism for a calorie deficit rather than an end in itself; the surrounding discussion concerns protein intake, training and whether the face looks gaunt or lean at the resulting body-fat level.
